title: Snakes, a Bronze Pole, and Battles
overview: On the last stretch of their desert journey, the Israelites complain and are struck by deadly snakes, are healed by looking at a bronze snake, and then defeat the kings who block their way east of the Jordan River.

parts.label: Victory at Hormah (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: When a Canaanite king attacks and takes captives, Israel vows that if God gives them victory they will completely destroy his towns and keep nothing for themselves. The text says they did, and the place was named Hormah, a name tied to the Hebrew word for this kind of total destruction.

parts.label: Complaints and deadly snakes (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Forced on a long detour around Edom, the worn-out people complain about the lack of water and call the manna, their daily food in the desert, miserable. The text presents the venomous snakes as God's judgment, and the people admit their wrong and ask Moses to pray for them.

parts.label: The bronze snake (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: God does not remove the snakes but provides a cure: a bronze snake on a pole that anyone bitten can look at and live. Centuries later people worshiped this object, so a king destroyed it, and Christians read it as a picture of Jesus being lifted up on the cross (John 3:14-15).

parts.label: Camps, songs and a well (vv. 10-20)
parts.note: This list of stops traces Israel's route north along the edge of Moab, quoting a lost early collection of poems to mark where the border lay. At Beer, a name meaning "well," God gives water and the people sing a short song celebrating the leaders who dug it.

parts.label: Defeat of King Sihon (vv. 21-32)
parts.note: Israel asks peacefully to pass along the main trade road, but Sihon attacks, loses, and Israel takes his land and his capital, Heshbon. The poem seems to be an older song about Sihon's own conquest of Moab, whose god was Chemosh, reused here to mark Israel's victory over Sihon, though scholars are unsure exactly how its lines divide.

parts.label: Defeat of King Og (vv. 33-35)
parts.note: God tells Moses not to fear Og, king of the fertile region of Bashan, and Israel kills him, his sons and his army with no survivors. These victories gave Israel its first settled territory, east of the Jordan.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ on how to understand the accounts of total destruction in this chapter, some reading them as literal commands of God for that moment and others as stylized or exaggerated war language from an ancient culture.
think: Have you ever found that facing something painful directly helped more than avoiding it, and why might that be?
